args.text:
On Saturday, the family of American muso and songwriter Bob Weir announced that he had died surrounded by loved ones. The former guitarist and singer with rock band the Grateful Dead was 78. His family announced his death on Instagram, saying he had recently battled a cancer diagnosis but died of "underlying lung issues". The announcement didn't say what day Weir died.

Weir played rhythm guitar and sang with American psychedelic rock band the Grateful Dead for decades, and wrote some of their songs too, including the hit "Sugar Magnolia", a fixture at Grateful Dead gigs. He also had a long solo career, putting together a string of bands with other Grateful Dead old boys, and kept playing live until a few months before his death.

Weir was born Robert Hall Parber on 16 October 1947 in San Francisco, California, and grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area, spending a stint at school in Colorado, where he met future Grateful Dead member John Perry Barlow. Weir took up guitar at 13 and drifted into the local bluegrass scene, where he first came across Jerry Garcia playing banjo. On 31 December 1965, Garcia and Weir agreed to start their own band, Mother McCree's Uptown Jug Champions, which grew into the Grateful Dead.

Weir played rhythm guitar, and sang, for the band for decades. From the 1970s he also tried his hand at a solo career and a swag of other bands outside the Grateful Dead, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, Furthur, The Other Ones, The Dead, Wolf Bros, and Dead & Company. Every one of them featured fellow Grateful Dead collaborators, and between them they covered everything from country rock to jam band to jazz-tinged roots rock built on blues and country. On vocals he mostly stuck to harmonies and backing, but he took the lead on a fair few tracks, including Grateful Dead anthem "Truckin'", a song the Library of Congress named a national treasure in 1997.

Away from the stage, Weir also set up Tamalpais Research Institute, a virtual performance platform, and was active in politics, backing a number of causes, including the environment, poverty relief, and issues to do with the arts. He'd stayed a regular on the Bay Area music scene, playing live with local musos and co-owning the venue Sweetwater Music Hall in Mill Valley, California.
